Analysis: Both hypotheses creatively propose a role for cancer-derived tRNA fragments delivered via exosomes in reprogramming tumor-associated macrophages, but key differences influence their overall merit. Hypothesis 1 focuses on the direct alteration of cytokine translation. It is straightforward in its claim but lacks precise details on which cytokines are targeted or the exact molecular interactions. In contrast, Hypothesis 2 introduces the added element of stress-induced production of tRFs—a nuance that naturally aligns with the high-stress environment of tumors—and extends the consequence to include metastasis. This extra dimension not only adds novelty but also improves the plausibility by linking known stress responses in cancer cells with subsequent exosomal signaling. Although both suffer from similar criticisms concerning mechanistic clarity and specific identification of tRFs, the integration of stress dynamics and metastasis in Hypothesis 2 renders it marginally more inventive and contextually grounded. Its testability, while requiring rigorous experimental design to isolate tRF effects amidst other exosomal molecules, offers clearer handles such as stress condition manipulations and comparative assays. Safety concerns are minimal and comparable for both. Overall, the additional layer of context provided by stress-induced generation in Hypothesis 2 tips the scales in its favor.
